newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire premier's own backers withdraw support.
newsitem.headline: Zaire premier's own backers withdraw support.

text.p: A part of the opposition alliance which helped bring Zaire's radical politician Etienne Tshisekedi back to power said on Saturday it had withdrawn its support for the new prime minister.
Tshisekedi has drawn fire from political opponents as well as his own backers in parliament by deciding to dissolve the legislature and appoint ministers by decree.

A spokesman for the Sacred Union opposition alliance said the group endorsed steps to remove Tshisekedi from office begun by the Presidential Movement which dominates parliament and groups President Mobutu Sese Seko's supporters.

"The opposition alliance upholds the accusations made by the presidential movement and takes note of the charges brought against the prime minister Mr Etienne Tshisekedi wa Mulumba," an opposition spokesman, Alexei Likango, declared after a meeting.
This meant members of a committee of opposition deputies assembled at parliament on Saturday had withdrawn support for the prime minister only days after he took office, lawmakers said.
However a complicated constitutional procedure to dismiss Tshisekedi may take up to two weeks, they added.

The meeting was held up for several hours by a group of about 50 pro-Tshisekedi demonstrators who carried placards declaring support for the prime minister. Civil guardsmen dispersed them peacefully but not before they had frightened off organisers of the meeting.

Later militant Tshisekedi supporters grouped together as they do daily in the capital's working class district of Matonge said they would continue to block parliament should procedures to dismiss their man continue.
Tshisekedi was named prime minister by an overwhelming majority of opposition parties last Monday. Mobut, who sacked him from the same job in 1993, then ratified the nomination of his arch-rival.
Mobutu's supporters initiated moves to remove Tshisekedi soon after he announced the controversial policy moves on his first day on the job on Thursday.
The Mobutu camp was completely excluded from the government unveiled by Tshisekedi the same day, as were opposition parties not affiliated to Tshisekedi's UDPS party.
In a separate development state radio said Tshisekedi supported talks which opened in South Africa on Saturday in hopes of ending six months of civil war in Zaire.
"The prime minister does not dispute the talks taking place in South Africa," the radio said, quoting South African ambassador Jan van de Venter who met Tshisekedi on Saturday.

"But he (Tshisekedi) thinks that since the problem is mainly between Zaireans, the authorities in Kinshasa should have taken the initiative to show to the rest of the world that Zaireans are able to solve their own problems," the radio quoted the envoy as saying.

On Thursday Tshisekedi dismissed the talks between official and rebel representatives as "useless". He said he planned his own talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila whose forces hold more than a third of Zaire territory.
